review.note: The 1960 convention, the special annex for Portugal and the share of 1960s industrial growth attributed to membership were written from memory, not read in the cited works.

summary: The free trade association founded by the Stockholm Convention of 1960 among the western European states that stayed outside the Common Market. Portugal was a founding member and by a wide margin the poorest of them, and the convention carried a special annex allowing it to keep protection for industries it was still building and to lower its tariffs on a longer schedule than the others. Joining committed the Estado Novo, which had governed a deliberately closed economy for thirty years, to opening it by stages; most accounts of the industrial growth of the 1960s give the association some of the credit and then argue about how much. Portugal stayed a member until it entered the European Communities on 1 January 1986. It is in the atlas because it is where the choice between Europe and the empire first had to be made in economic terms rather than rhetorical ones.
